subject: physics

moments.title: Ørsted finds magnetism from current
moments.body:
Ørsted, lecturing on electricity, notices that a compass needle near a wire deflects when current flows through the wire. Electric current produces a magnetic field. Within months, Ampère in Paris quantifies the effect.

The symmetric question is open: can a magnetic field produce a current? Many try; none succeed. Faraday, an apprentice bookbinder turned chemist at the Royal Institution, takes up the problem.
moments.takeaway: Half the connection between electricity and magnetism is established. The other half is a 11-year puzzle.

moments.title: Faraday's induction
moments.body:
On 29 August 1831 Faraday wraps two coils of wire on opposite sides of an iron ring. Connecting one to a battery, he notices a brief deflection in a galvanometer on the other coil — but only when the battery is switched on or off, not while current flows steadily.

The insight: it's the CHANGE in magnetic flux that induces EMF, not the flux itself. Within months he demonstrates that moving a magnet in and out of a coil produces alternating current.

quote.text: I have had an electric eel.
quote.attrib: Michael Faraday, in another diary entry — but in 1831 he simply writes: 'The current sets in the contrary direction when the conjunction with the battery is broken.'

moments.takeaway: Changing magnetic flux drives EMF. The principle of every dynamo, transformer and motor is born.

moments.title: Lines of force become a field
moments.body:
Faraday has almost no mathematical training. He visualises electromagnetic phenomena as 'lines of force' filling space — invisible but real. He sprinkles iron filings on paper above a magnet and sees the lines made visible. He pictures the field, not action-at-a-distance, as the medium of force.

Most mathematicians of his era dismiss the picture as unrigorous. Maxwell will take it seriously.

quote.text: The lines of force, then, are conditions of the surrounding space, and not particular lines.
quote.attrib: Michael Faraday, Experimental Researches in Electricity, Vol. III

moments.takeaway: Faraday invents the concept of a field. Mathematics catches up to him 30 years later.

moments.title: Maxwell mathematises Faraday's intuition
moments.body:
Maxwell publishes 'A Dynamical Theory of the Electromagnetic Field' in 1865. He puts Faraday's lines of force into four differential equations governing electric and magnetic fields.

The equations predict electromagnetic waves travelling at exactly the speed of light. Light is an electromagnetic wave. Faraday's intuition, given mathematical form, unifies electromagnetism and optics.
moments.takeaway: Faraday's pictures and Maxwell's equations are the same physics, in different languages.

now.title: Induction today
now.body:
Faraday's induction underpins every motor, generator, transformer, induction cooker and wireless phone charger. World electric grids depend on it.

Induction is also the principle behind eddy-current braking (used in trains, roller coasters and laboratory dampers) and inductive heating (used in metallurgy and welding).
now.open_questions: Can wireless power transfer scale up to charge vehicles in motion on roads, and to charge implanted medical devices for life? Can superconducting motors and generators (which exploit zero ohmic loss) replace conventional machines economically?

reflection: Faraday left school at 13 and worked as a bookbinder's apprentice. He had no university degree. He became Director of the Royal Institution, gave the Christmas Lectures for decades, and changed physics. How does science deal with self-taught outsiders compared with formally trained insiders?
